extracted.intended_audience: IP practitioners, patent applicants, policymakers and statisticians
extracted.subtask_description: Definitions and procedural/eligibility criteria across major IP systems (patents, utility models, trademarks, industrial designs, plant varieties, geographical indications) and related international registration systems (PCT, Madrid, Hague, Lisbon, Budapest). Useful for applicants, examiners and analysts comparing filings/rights across jurisdictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: To qualify for patent protection, an invention must be novel, involve an inventive step (non-obviousness) and be industrially applicable. A patent confers exclusive rights for a limited period (generally 20 years).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants must disclose the invention so others skilled in the art may replicate it. The substantive determination of novelty, inventive step and industrial applicability is made by national or regional patent offices under their national laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent disclosure and filing procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants obtain patent rights by filing an application describing the invention with a national or regional office. Applicants may also file an international application through the PCT System.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The PCT process has an international phase (international search, optional preliminary examination and supplementary international search) and concludes with a national phase where national/regional offices decide patentability according to national law. The PCT simplifies timing for multiple national filings but grant decisions remain national.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility model eligibility and characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: A utility model (UM) confers exclusive rights like a patent but terms and conditions differ: UMs are typically issued for a shorter period (6–10 years) and at most offices protection is granted without substantive examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The term 'utility model' here includes similar protections (e.g., innovation patents in Australia, short-term patents in Ireland). Procedures and substantive requirements vary by national/regional office and rights are jurisdiction-limited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure requirement for microorganisms (Budapest Treaty)
rubrics_metrics.description: When an invention involves microorganisms, disclosure may require depositing a sample at a designated International Depositary Authority (IDA).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under the Budapest Treaty, deposit with any IDA suffices for patent procedures in all contracting states and regional patent offices that recognize the Treaty, eliminating the need to deposit in every country where protection is sought. As of July 2020 there are 48 IDAs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plant variety protection criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: A breeder’s right is granted only when a variety is new, distinct, uniform and stable, and has a suitable denomination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To obtain protection, a plant breeder must file an individual application with each authority granting breeders' rights. Different national frameworks exist (e.g., U.S. PPA covers asexually reproduced distinct new varieties; PVPA covers sexually reproduced and tuber-propagated varieties, excluding fungi and bacteria).

rubrics_metrics.name: Trademark function and maintenance
rubrics_metrics.description: A trademark is a sign used to distinguish the goods or services of one enterprise from another; the holder of a registered trademark has the exclusive right to use the mark for the goods/services for which it is registered and can block unauthorized or confusingly similar use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trademark registrations can be maintained indefinitely provided renewal fees are paid. Rights are limited to the jurisdiction of registration. Registration procedures are governed by national/regional laws and national offices retain the decision to register even in international filings (e.g., Madrid System).

rubrics_metrics.name: Madrid System filing and management features
rubrics_metrics.description: The Madrid System allows trademark holders to submit a single international application in one language (English, French or Spanish), pay a single set of fees (in Swiss francs), and designate Madrid members where protection is sought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The System simplifies subsequent management (central recording of changes, renewals). A registration in the International Register yields the same effect as a direct registration in each designated Contracting Party unless the competent national/regional authority issues a refusal within a specified period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industrial design protectability
rubrics_metrics.description: Industrial designs refer to the ornamental or aesthetic aspects of a useful article (lines, colors, three-dimensional forms) and can be protected if they are new or original.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Holders of a registered industrial design have exclusive rights to prevent unauthorized copying or imitation. The term of protection is generally five-year renewable periods up to about 15 years in most jurisdictions, though some (e.g., China) provide a 10-year term from the application date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hague System international design filing and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: The Hague System allows an applicant to register industrial designs in multiple territories by filing a single application with WIPO and permits up to 100 different designs per application (for products in the same class).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The System simplifies multinational registration and subsequent management (recording changes, renewals centrally). Whether an application may contain multiple designs and the number allowed varies across national/regional offices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hague System entitlement criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Entitlement to file an international application under the Hague Agreement is limited to natural persons or legal entities with a real and effective industrial or commercial establishment, domicile, nationality, or (under the 1999 Act) habitual residence in a Contracting Party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eligibility rules differ between the Hague Act (1960) and the Geneva Act (1999); applicants must meet the applicable entitlement basis to file internationally under the Hague route.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographical indication (GI) core requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A geographical indication is a sign identifying a good as originating in a specific geographical area and possessing a given quality, reputation or other characteristic essentially attributable to that geographical origin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: GIs can only be used on goods that conform to applicable requirements concerning area of origin, processing method and typicity. Goods produced outside the area or not meeting these requirements are prevented from using the protected indication. GI rights are territorial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appellation of origin stronger GI standard
rubrics_metrics.description: An appellation of origin is a sub-category of GI where the quality or characteristics of the product are due exclusively or essentially to the geographical environment, including natural and human factors — requiring a stronger link to place than other GIs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appellations of origin are more restrictive than general GIs; they typically consist of a geographical name or traditional denomination and denote products whose qualities are primarily attributable to their territory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection mechanisms for GIs
rubrics_metrics.description: GIs are protected through various national/regional legal means: sui generis GI laws (registration-based), trademark law (collective and certification marks), unfair competition/consumer protection laws, administrative and judicial decisions, or specific decrees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sui generis and trademark-based protections are not mutually exclusive and may coexist. Protection obtained in one jurisdiction is limited territorially; international/regional agreements and WIPO systems (Lisbon, Madrid) can facilitate protection abroad.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lisbon System features for appellations of origin/GIs
rubrics_metrics.description: The Lisbon System provides a single registration procedure administered by WIPO to facilitate international protection of appellations of origin (and under the Geneva Act, GIs) so that registration with the International Bureau ensures protection in all Lisbon contracting parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protection under Lisbon continues while the appellation/GI remains protected in its country of origin. Each contracting party can refuse protection within one year of notification based on national/regional grounds. The Geneva Act (2015) extended scope and membership flexibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical counting: equivalent applications and grants
rubrics_metrics.description: Applications/grants at regional offices are treated as equivalent to multiple national filings/grants — one per member state — for reporting data by origin. Calculation rules vary by office (e.g., BOIP, EAPO, EUIPO, GCC, OAPI multiply by member states; EPO and ARIPO have different resident/non-resident counting rules).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These equivalency concepts are used to report and compare data by origin. Analysts must apply office-specific conversion rules when aggregating world totals to avoid miscounting regional filings/grants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical unit definitions: class count and design count
rubrics_metrics.description: Class count is the number of Nice Classification classes specified in a trademark application; design count is the number of designs contained in an industrial design application. These counts are used to capture differences across offices (multi-class vs single-class filing systems; single vs multiple designs per application).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use class and design counts when comparing application/registration numbers across offices to better reflect filing scope differences (some offices require separate single-class filings; others permit multi-class filings or multiple designs per application).

rubrics_metrics.name: Application date and filing definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Application date (filing date) is the date on which the IP office receives an application that meets the minimum requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This date is the reference for many procedural deadlines and for statistical reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant for statistical origin determination
rubrics_metrics.description: For statistical purposes in this publication, the name of the first named applicant is used to determine the origin of the application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There may be multiple applicants; using the first named applicant provides a consistent rule for attributing origin in aggregate statistics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of invention
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention is a new solution to a technical problem; to qualify for patent protection it must be novel, involve an inventive step and be industrially applicable, as judged by a person skilled in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This summarizes the substantive standard examiners apply when assessing patent applications.
